question: Does adding redundant ReLU student neurons slow gradient descent when the target is exactly one ReLU under Gaussian population loss?

key_findings.claim: For two or more student neurons learning one teacher ReLU, randomly initialized gradient descent globally converges at order T^-3 under stringent dimension, initialization, and step-size conditions.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 9 formalizes the upper bound with d logarithmic in n/delta, extremely small Gaussian initialization, and polynomially small learning rate; it is presented as the first global result beyond matched one- and two-neuron special cases.

key_findings.claim: A matching order T^-3 gradient-flow lower bound makes the polynomial rate exact in the analyzed regime.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 12 bounds loss below by a constant-shifted inverse cubic for all time with high probability, whereas matched single-neuron gradient descent has established exponential convergence.

key_findings.claim: The global proof decomposes training into three phases and shows implicit balancing among student neurons.
key_findings.evidence: Phase 1 grows initially tiny neurons, Phase 2 aligns them toward the teacher and controls residual error, and Phase 3 maintains individual norms between constant multiples of teacher norm divided by n while an improved gradient lower bound drives loss down.

key_findings.claim: Slow convergence arises from the gradual collapse of pairwise differences between redundant neurons.
key_findings.evidence: The lower-bound potential sums pairwise distances. Once neurons are aligned and balanced, homogeneity and non-smooth interactions make this diversity decay slowly, which prevents the population loss from falling faster than inverse cubic.

key_findings.claim: The phrase exponentially slows down compares exponential-in-iterations matched convergence with polynomial-in-iterations redundant convergence, not an exponential dependence on width.
key_findings.evidence: Both over-parameterized upper and lower rates are T^-3 with constants depending polynomially or worse on n and initialization; the qualitative gap is between exp(-Omega(T)) and inverse polynomial time.

key_findings.claim: The result is a sharply controlled counterexample, not evidence that over-parameterization generally slows deep-network training.
key_findings.evidence: It uses one positive-output ReLU teacher, an unweighted sum of student ReLUs, exact Gaussian population expectation, square loss, no output signs or biases, and exceptionally small initialization. Finite samples, SGD, representation mismatch, and realistic depth are absent.

method.core_idea: Analyze exact gradient dynamics of redundant homogeneous ReLU neurons and prove matching inverse-cubic upper and lower loss rates.
method.mechanism: Gaussian integration gives a closed population objective in neuron norms and angles. Phase invariants establish growth, alignment, and norm balance; a gradient dominance inequality yields the upper rate. A pairwise-distance potential quantifies redundancy and supplies the lower rate under gradient flow.
assumptions: Inputs are standard Gaussian and labels come from exactly one bias-free ReLU.
Student output is an unweighted sum of n ReLUs with positive homogeneity.
Initialization is independent Gaussian at a very small scale and dimension grows at least logarithmically with width and confidence.
Population square loss and full-batch gradient methods model the relevant optimization behavior.

techniques.role: Expresses loss and gradients through norms and pairwise angles.
Separates neuron growth, teacher alignment, and asymptotic convergence.
Bounds every student norm near the teacher norm divided by width.
Improves gradient dominance sufficiently to integrate an inverse-cubic upper rate.
Shows redundant neurons cannot merge quickly enough for faster loss convergence.

evaluations.setting: Analytical teacher-student population loss with one teacher and n Gaussian-initialized student ReLUs.
evaluations.result: Under explicit initialization and learning-rate scalings, loss is upper bounded by a polynomial constant times T^-3.
evaluations.baseline: Known exponential convergence for an exactly parameterized one-neuron student.

evaluations.setting: The same over-parameterized problem under continuous gradient flow.
evaluations.result: Loss is at least (Gamma1 T + Gamma2)^-3, matching the upper exponent.
evaluations.baseline: The exact-parameterized flow and the paper's own upper rate.

evaluations.setting: Numerical population-gradient dynamics across student widths.
evaluations.result: Widths n>=2 show substantially slower decay and slopes trending toward -3, while n=1 decays linearly on the semilog scale.

limitations: The extremely small initialization and learning-rate exponents make the formal constants impractical.
Only one ReLU teacher, positive fixed output weights, Gaussian inputs, and population square loss are covered.
The lower bound is for gradient flow, while the upper bound is for discrete gradient descent.
No stochastic gradients, finite datasets, biases, noise, depth, or modern optimization components are studied.
The theorem does not show a monotonic width-dependent slowdown beyond the qualitative n=1 versus n>=2 split.
failure_modes: Signed or trainable output weights may let redundant neurons cancel or specialize and remove the slow pairwise-collapse mechanism.
Larger initialization can begin outside the three-phase invariant region.
Non-Gaussian or finite inputs can change the angular kernel and introduce spurious minima or faster routes.
SGD noise can break symmetry between redundant neurons and alter the asymptotic rate.
The width-dependent constants may dominate before any T^-3 asymptotic regime becomes visible.
reusable_insights: Test benefits of over-parameterization against optimization time, not only global convergence or attainable loss.
Track pairwise diversity among redundant units as a potential source of slow asymptotics.
Clarify whether 'exponential slowdown' refers to time-rate class or dependence on model size.
Use matched lower and upper rates to distinguish a proof artifact from a genuine dynamical bottleneck.
open_questions: Does the inverse-cubic slowdown persist with trainable signed output weights or multiple teachers?
How do finite samples and SGD noise affect redundant-neuron collapse?
Can a symmetry-breaking regularizer or merge operation restore exponential convergence?
Which practical architectures exhibit an analogous redundancy potential at observable timescales?

competitive_landscape.title: Learning ReLUs via Gradient Descent
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational exact-parameterization linear-convergence result under Gaussian design.
competitive_landscape.difference: Soltanolkotabi studies a properly specified single ReLU with projected GD; Xu and Du show that representing the same target with redundant positive ReLUs changes the asymptotic rate to inverse cubic.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning a Single Neuron with Gradient Methods
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest prior matched-width analysis of single-neuron gradient convergence.
competitive_landscape.difference: The prior work proves conditions for learning one neuron properly; this paper focuses on interactions and exact rates when multiple student neurons redundantly learn it.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Tangent Kernel: Convergence and Generalization in Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Contrasting theory in which infinite width linearizes training and supports fast convergence.
competitive_landscape.difference: NTK results use parameterizations and regimes where a stable kernel drives optimization; the single-neuron construction uses positive homogeneous redundant units whose slow mutual coalescence dominates.

competitive_landscape.title: Spurious Local Minima are Common in Two-Layer ReLU Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Competing account of optimization difficulty in shallow teacher-student ReLU networks.
competitive_landscape.difference: Safran and Shamir emphasize bad stationary geometry for broader multi-neuron targets; Xu and Du prove global convergence but identify a slow asymptotic rate even without failure to reach a global optimum.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The work gives the first global gradient-descent result beyond exact parameterization for this problem and proves that even mild over-parameterization changes exponential convergence to an exact inverse-cubic rate.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The matching rate and redundancy potential make a clean counterexample to the slogan that width always speeds optimization. Its scientific value is conceptual rather than directly predictive: the parameterization and asymptotic assumptions are unusually narrow and the formal constants extreme.

reviewer_notes: Read the complete 43-page extraction, including setup, all three phase theorems, gradient bound, formal global result, toy lower-bound cases, pairwise potential, and proof appendices. Four primary arXiv optimization theories were checked on 2026-08-23.
